title: Ancient Greek placement diagnostic, stage 1
notes: Item bank for docs/greek-diagnostic-spec.md. Sources, choices, verification and per-item doubts: content/grc/diagnostic/authoring-notes.md. Unlisted items p2b, p2b-q1–q6 and w1b replace p2, p2-q1–q6 and w1 when the learner has read Anabasis 3.

sections.title: About you
sections.intro_en: Before any Greek: a few questions about what you have read, so the test can avoid passages you already know. Then one untimed practice round to get used to typing Greek. Allow about 35 minutes initially; you can stop at a section boundary and resume. Taking longer does not lower your placement.

sections.title: Reading
sections.intro_en: Two passages of Xenophon, the first written for this test, the second as he wrote it. Read each at your own pace; the text stays on screen while you answer, and rereading is expected. If a question can't be answered, leave it rather than guess.

sections.title: Where did you get stuck?
sections.intro_en: Mark up to five places where your reading stopped, and say what you think they mean, even if that is 'no idea'. Help then arrives in steps: a few word meanings, then the shape of the sentence, then a translation.

sections.title: Forms in context
sections.intro_en: Short sentences, each with one decision that changes the meaning, then eight gaps to fill. Accents and breathings are optional when you type.

sections.title: Words
sections.intro_en: Fourteen words, each in a short phrase. Pick the meaning and say how sure you are; 'unknown' is a perfectly good answer.

sections.title: Writing Greek
sections.intro_en: Three short pieces of Greek and an optional fourth. The passages are there to borrow from. What matters first is that the meaning comes across; the forms are looked at separately.

sections.title: Optional: Plato
sections.intro_en: About five minutes: Socrates thinking aloud in the Apology.

sections.title: Optional: Aeschylus
sections.intro_en: About five minutes: the watchman who opens the Agamemnon. Poetic words are glossed with their everyday prose equivalents.

practice.label: Practice
practice.source: written for this test (after Athenaze ch. 1)
practice.context_en: A warm-up: two sentences about an old friend from Athenaze.

sentences.translation_en: Dicaeopolis walks to the field;
and Xanthias drives the oxen.

options: Xanthias
Dicaeopolis
Dicaeopolis and Xanthias together
Nobody: the oxen are walking to the field
why: Right: ὁ δὲ Ξανθίας is the subject of ἐλαύνει.
Dicaeopolis is walking to the field; ὁ δέ switches to a new subject.
Each sentence has its own subject and verb.
τοὺς βοῦς is accusative: the oxen are being driven.

practice.prompt_en: Select the words that say where Dicaeopolis is going.

p1.label: At the ford (written for this test, after Xenophon)
p1.source: new Attic narrative written for this diagnostic in the manner of Xenophon's Anabasis
p1.context_en: A new passage written in Xenophon's style. A Greek army marching through hostile country has come to a river.

sentences.translation_en: When the Greeks reached the river, it looked deep and nowhere fordable.
Since everyone was at a loss, the general sent a captain with twenty peltasts to look for a ford.
They, marching along the river, come to a small village, and there they catch an old man hiding in a house.
They asked him whether the river was fordable anywhere.
He said that there was a ford not far upstream, but that it was guarded by horsemen.
Having heard this, the captain ordered him to lead the way, and they marched through the night.
At daybreak, while the horsemen were still asleep, the peltasts went into the river.
The water came up to their chests;
and, holding their shields above their heads, they made their way across.
The horsemen, woken by the noise, when they saw them already in the middle of the river, leapt onto their horses and fled.
The captain, having crossed, sent one of the peltasts to the general to report that the ford was unguarded.
As for the old man, since he had proved trustworthy, he gave him gifts and let him go.

p1-q1.prompt_en: What happens in this passage, in brief?
options: A small party sent ahead finds a ford with a local man's help and gets across it.
The whole army crosses the river by night at a ford the local man shows them.
A local man leads the scouting party into an ambush, and they barely escape.
The scouts fail to find a ford and return to the general with a prisoner.
why: Right: twenty peltasts under a captain, an old man who knows the ford, a crossing at dawn.
Only the scouting party crosses; the army is still with the general, who is sent a message.
The old man tells the truth (he 'proved trustworthy') and is rewarded.
They do find a ford and cross it; the old man is let go.
p1-q1.ablation: The gist depends on following the chain of main verbs (ἔπεμψε, ἀφικνοῦνται, λαμβάνουσιν, εἰσέβησαν, διέβαινον, ἔφυγον, ἀφῆκεν); a reader who loses the main clauses among the participles cannot tell who crossed or whether the guide was loyal.

p1-q2.prompt_en: On their way to the village, which way did the scouting party march?
options: Along the river
Away from the river, inland
Across the river to the far bank
Down to the river from the hills
why: Right: παρά + accusative with a verb of motion = along, beside (παρὰ τὸν ποταμόν).
'From the river' would need παρά + genitive (or ἀπό); here the case is accusative.
Crossing comes later (εἰσέβησαν, διέβαινον); 'across' would be διά or πέραν.
Motion to the river would be ἐπί / πρὸς τὸν ποταμόν; they are already at it.
p1-q2.ablation: Only the case after παρά decides between 'along' (accusative) and 'from beside' (genitive); the story itself makes 'away from' or 'to' the river equally plausible.

p1-q3.prompt_en: In φυλάττεσθαι δὲ αὐτὸν and then ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ἡγεῖσθαι, whom or what does αὐτόν refer to each time?
options: First the ford; then the old man
First the old man; then the ford
The ford in both places
The old man in both places
why: The ford is guarded; the captain orders the old man to guide them.
This reverses the two references.
The second αὐτόν is the person ordered to guide the party.
The first αὐτόν refers back to πόρον.
p1-q3.ablation: The two identical forms must each be resolved from their roles: the first is subject of the passive infinitive φυλάττεσθαι in the old man's report (picking up πόρον), the second is object of ἐκέλευσεν and subject of ἡγεῖσθαι (the old man). Without tracking reference, B–D are equally available.

p1-q4.prompt_en: At daybreak, when the peltasts went into the river, what was the situation?
options: The horsemen were still asleep as the peltasts went in.
The peltasts were still half asleep as they went in.
The peltasts went in and then waited for the horsemen to fall asleep.
The peltasts went in so as to catch the horsemen asleep.
why: Right: τῶν ἱππέων ἔτι καθευδόντων is a genitive absolute with its own subject, the horsemen.
The sleeping belongs to τῶν ἱππέων (genitive), not to the nominative οἱ πελτασταί.
ἔτι καθευδόντων: the horsemen were already, and still, asleep; nothing is waited for.
A genitive absolute gives circumstance, not purpose; the text says only that they were asleep.
p1-q4.ablation: If τῶν ἱππέων … καθευδόντων is not read as a genitive absolute with its own subject, the sleeping can be pinned on the peltasts (B) or read as an aim (D).

p1-q5.prompt_en: Select the words that say what the horsemen saw.
p1-q5.why: αὐτοὺς ἤδη ἐν μέσῳ τῷ ποταμῷ ὄντας: 'them (the peltasts) already in the middle of the river'. The participle ὄντας after a verb of seeing gives what was seen.
p1-q5.ablation: The object of εἶδον is the accusative-and-participle phrase αὐτοὺς … ὄντας; without recognising the supplementary participle, readers stop at αὐτούς or run on into ἀναπηδήσαντες.

p1-q6.prompt_en: Who let the old man go, and why?
options: The captain, because the old man had proved trustworthy
The peltast sent to the general, because the old man had proved trustworthy
The captain, because the old man had guided him to the general
The captain, because the old man had given him gifts
why: Right: ἀφῆκεν has no expressed subject, so it carries on from ὁ λοχαγός; ἐπεὶ πιστὸς ἐφάνη gives the reason.
ἕνα τῶν πελταστῶν is the object of ἔπεμψεν in the previous sentence, not the new subject.
The old man guided them to the ford; the general is not where they are.
δοὺς is nominative singular, like the subject of ἀφῆκεν: the captain gave the gifts.
p1-q6.ablation: ἀφῆκεν has no expressed subject; it must be carried over from ὁ λοχαγός past the accusatives ἕνα τῶν πελταστῶν and τὸν στρατηγόν. Ignore that and the peltast or the general are live candidates.

p2.label: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.1.4–7
p2.context_en: Here Xenophon, the author, first brings himself into his own story.

sentences.translation_en: There was in the army a certain Xenophon, an Athenian, who was going along neither as general nor as captain nor as soldier; rather, Proxenus had sent for him from home, being an old guest-friend of his;
And he was promising him that, if he came, he would make him a friend to Cyrus, who, he himself said, was worth more to him than his homeland.
Xenophon, however, having read the letter, consults Socrates the Athenian about the journey.

tokens.gloss: open to blame, a ground for accusation

sentences.translation_en: And Socrates, suspecting that becoming a friend to Cyrus might be something the city would hold against him, because Cyrus was thought to have eagerly joined the Spartans in their war against Athens, advises Xenophon to go to Delphi and consult the god about the journey.

Having gone there, Xenophon asked Apollo to which of the gods he should sacrifice and pray in order to make the journey he had in mind in the finest and best way, and to come home safe after faring well.
And Apollo answered him with the gods to whom he had to sacrifice.
When he came back, he tells the oracle's reply to Socrates.

And he, having heard it, blamed him because he had not first asked this—whether it was better for him to go or to stay—but, having decided by himself that he must go, was inquiring this: how he might go in the finest way.
'Since, however, you did ask it this way,' he said, 'you must do whatever the god ordered.'

p2-q1.prompt_en: What happens in this passage, in brief?
options: Xenophon, invited to join Cyrus, consults Socrates and then the oracle, and reports back to Socrates.
Xenophon, ordered by Cyrus to join him, consults the oracle, which forbids the journey.
Socrates, invited to join Cyrus, sends Xenophon to Delphi to ask the god on his behalf.
Xenophon consults Socrates, who persuades him to stay at home rather than join Cyrus.
why: Right: Proxenus's letter, Socrates's advice, the visit to Delphi, the return to Socrates.
The invitation comes from Proxenus, and the oracle names gods to sacrifice to; it forbids nothing.
The invitation is to Xenophon (αὐτὸν μετεπέμψατο), and Xenophon asks for himself.
Socrates sends him to Delphi and finally tells him to do what the god ordered.
p2-q1.ablation: The gist depends on following the main verbs (μετεπέμψατο, ἀνακοινοῦται, συμβουλεύει, ἐπήρετο, ἀνεῖλεν, λέγει, ᾐτιᾶτο) through long participial and subordinate material.

options: That if Xenophon came, he would make him a friend of Cyrus
That if Xenophon came, Cyrus would make him a general
That since Xenophon had come, he had already made him Cyrus's friend
That if Xenophon became Cyrus's friend, Proxenus himself would come
why: Right: ποιήσειν is a future infinitive after ὑπισχνεῖτο, with the condition εἰ ἔλθοι.
The subject of ποιήσειν is Proxenus (unexpressed, same as the main verb), and the promise is friendship, not a command.
ποιήσειν is future: a promise, not something already done; εἰ ἔλθοι is a condition, not a cause.
εἰ ἔλθοι belongs to Xenophon coming; φίλον αὐτὸν Κύρῳ ποιήσειν is what Proxenus would do.
p2-q2.ablation: The promise is carried by the future infinitive ποιήσειν with its reported condition εἰ ἔλθοι; without that, promise and accomplished fact (C), and who does what (D), cannot be told apart.

p2-q3.prompt_en: What did Proxenus say he himself thought?
options: That Cyrus was worth more to him than his own homeland
That Cyrus thought Proxenus worth more to him than his own homeland
That Xenophon would find Cyrus worth more to him than his homeland
That his homeland was worth more to him than Cyrus
why: Right: ὃν = Cyrus (object), αὐτός and ἑαυτῷ = Proxenus, τῆς πατρίδος = 'than his homeland'.
ὃν is accusative: Cyrus is the one being valued, not the one valuing.
αὐτὸς ἔφη: Proxenus is speaking about his own view; Xenophon is not the subject.
τῆς πατρίδος is a genitive of comparison after κρείττω: the homeland is what Cyrus is worth more than.
p2-q3.ablation: ὃν (accusative) must be taken back to Κύρῳ, αὐτός/ἑαυτῷ to Proxenus, and τῆς πατρίδος as a genitive of comparison; drop the relative's case and B is as good as A.

options: That becoming Cyrus's friend might be held against Xenophon by Athens
That becoming Cyrus's friend would not be held against Xenophon by Athens
That Cyrus might hold it against Xenophon that he was an Athenian
That Xenophon's friendship might lead Cyrus to make war on Athens
why: Right: μή after ὑποπτεύσας introduces a feared possibility, 'that perhaps … might', with πρὸς τῆς πόλεως 'in the eyes of the city'.
μή here is not a plain 'not': after a verb of suspecting or fearing it means 'that (perhaps)'.
πρὸς τῆς πόλεως: the blame would come from the city, not from Cyrus.
The ὅτι clause looks back: Cyrus was thought to have helped Sparta against Athens already.
p2-q4.ablation: μή after ὑποπτεύσας introduces a feared possibility ('that perhaps … might'), not a negation; reading μή as 'not' gives B.

p2-q5.prompt_en: Socrates says there was a question Xenophon should have asked first. Select the Greek words of that question.
p2-q5.why: πότερον λῷον εἴη αὐτῷ πορεύεσθαι ἢ μένειν: 'whether it was better for him to go or to stay'. What Xenophon actually asked was ὅπως ἂν κάλλιστα πορευθείη.
p2-q5.ablation: Two indirect questions compete (πότερον … μένειν and ὅπως … πορευθείη); only by seeing that οὐ τοῦτο πρῶτον ἠρώτα governs the first can one pick it, and the second (what Xenophon actually asked) is the tempting choice.

p2-q6.prompt_en: According to Socrates's complaint, who had already decided that the journey must be made?
options: Xenophon himself
Socrates
Apollo
Proxenus
why: Right: αὐτὸς κρίνας goes with ἐπυνθάνετο, whose subject is still Xenophon (the αὐτόν Socrates blamed).
Socrates is the subject of ᾐτιᾶτο; inside the ὅτι clause the subject is the man he blamed.
Apollo answered a question; the decision to go was taken before the question was put.
Proxenus invited him, but the 'deciding by himself' belongs to the one asking the oracle.
p2-q6.ablation: αὐτὸς κρίνας has no noun; it must be read as subject of ἐπυνθάνετο, which continues the subject of ἠρώτα (Xenophon, the αὐτόν of ᾐτιᾶτο). Without that tracking, Socrates (the nearest nominative, ὁ δ') is the natural guess.

r1.greek: οἱ δὲ στρατιῶται [[ἐπαύσαντο]] τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους βάλλοντες.
options: The soldiers stopped pelting the prisoners.
The soldiers stopped the prisoners from pelting them.
The prisoners made the soldiers stop pelting.
The soldiers, while pelting, stopped the prisoners.
why: Right: middle ἐπαύσαντο = 'stopped (themselves)'; the nominative participle βάλλοντες says what they stopped doing.
Stopping someone else would be active ἔπαυσαν with an accusative participle (τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους βάλλοντας).
οἱ στρατιῶται is the subject; the prisoners are the accusative object of βάλλοντες.
The participle gives the activity that ceased, not something done at the same time.
r1.ablation: Only the middle voice of ἐπαύσαντο (with the nominative participle) decides between 'stopped pelting' and 'stopped someone'.

r2.greek: ὁ δὲ Κλέαρχος ἔφη αὐτὸς [[ἀποκτενεῖν]] τὸν αἰχμάλωτον.
options: That he would kill the prisoner himself
That he had killed the prisoner himself
That he was killing the prisoner at that very moment
That the prisoner would kill him
why: Right: ἀποκτενεῖν is the contracted (liquid) future infinitive: 'that he would kill'.
'Had killed' would be the aorist infinitive ἀποκτεῖναι.
'Was killing' would be the present infinitive ἀποκτείνειν.
αὐτός (nominative) makes Clearchus the subject; τὸν αἰχμάλωτον is the object.
r2.ablation: The decision rests on recognising ἀποκτενεῖν as a liquid future (vs. aorist ἀποκτεῖναι, present ἀποκτείνειν); the rest of the sentence fits all three.

r3.greek: [[οἱ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ]], ὡς εἶδον τοὺς Ἕλληνας, ἔφυγον εἰς τὰ ὄρη.
options: The people in the village
The Greeks who were in the village
The Greeks, from the village
Both the Greeks and the villagers
why: Right: οἱ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ = 'those in the village'; they saw the Greeks and fled.
The Greeks are the object (τοὺς Ἕλληνας) of εἶδον; they are what was seen.
ἐν τῇ κώμῃ is attached to οἱ ('those in the village'), not to a verb of fleeing.
Only one subject is expressed: οἱ ἐν τῇ κώμῃ.
r3.ablation: The article οἱ turns the phrase ἐν τῇ κώμῃ into the subject ('those in the village'); ignore that and 'the Greeks in the village' (B, C) is a natural misreading.

r4.greek: ὁ στρατηγὸς ἐπῄνεσε τὸν λοχαγὸν [[ᾧ]] μάλιστα ἐπίστευεν.
options: The general praised the captain whom he trusted most.
The general praised the captain who trusted him most.
The general praised the captain and from then on trusted him most.
The general praised the captain because the captain trusted him.
why: Right: ᾧ is dative, the object of ἐπίστευεν (πιστεύω takes the dative); the general is the one trusting.
'Who trusted him' would need the nominative ὅς.
ᾧ is a relative pronoun linking to τὸν λοχαγόν, not 'and'.
A relative clause describes the captain; it gives no reason.
r4.ablation: Only the case of the relative (ᾧ, dative object of πιστεύω) decides who trusts whom; with ὅς the meaning would flip to B.

r5.greek: ὁ λοχαγὸς τῷ στρατηγῷ [[ἀπιόντι]] τὰ γενόμενα ἔλεγεν.
options: The general
The captain
Both the captain and the general
The men involved in what had happened
why: Right: ἀπιόντι is dative, agreeing with τῷ στρατηγῷ.
The captain is nominative (ὁ λοχαγός); a participle for him would be ἀπιών.
The participle is singular and dative: one person, the general.
τὰ γενόμενα is neuter: 'the things that had happened', not people.
r5.ablation: Only the dative case of ἀπιόντι attaches the leaving to the general; without it, the speaker (the captain) is the obvious guess.

r6.greek: ὁ δὲ Κλέαρχος ἔγνω [[ἐξηπατημένος]] ὑπὸ τοῦ Τισσαφέρνους.
options: That he had been deceived by Tissaphernes
That he had deceived Tissaphernes
That Tissaphernes was deceiving someone else
He realised it at the moment he was being deceived
why: Right: after ἔγνω, a nominative participle gives what the subject realised about himself; ἐξηπατημένος is perfect passive, with ὑπό + genitive for the agent.
The participle is passive (ὑπὸ τοῦ Τισσαφέρνους = by Tissaphernes).
The participle is nominative and agrees with Clearchus: he is the one deceived.
With γιγνώσκω, the participle gives the content of the realisation, not its timing.
r6.ablation: Reading ἐξηπατημένος as a supplementary participle (content of ἔγνω) rather than a circumstantial one is what turns 'he realised, being deceived' into 'he realised he had been deceived'.

r7.greek: οὕτω ταχέως ἐπορεύοντο [[ὥστε οὐδεὶς αὐτοὺς εἶδεν]].
r7.prompt_en: What does the underlined clause tell us?
options: That in fact no one saw them
What they were aiming at: that no one should see them
Why they marched so fast: no one had seen them
What would have happened if they had marched fast
why: Right: ὥστε with an indicative (εἶδεν) states an actual result.
Aim would be a purpose clause (ἵνα / ὅπως + subjunctive or optative).
A cause would be ὅτι or ἐπεί + indicative; ὥστε gives a consequence.
There is no ἄν and no condition; the clause states a fact.
r7.ablation: The indicative after ὥστε is what makes this an actual result; with the mood ignored, purpose (B) is just as natural in English.

r8.greek: εἰ μὴ νὺξ ἐπεγένετο, [[οὐκ ἂν ἐσώθησαν]] οἱ πελτασταί.
options: Yes: night came on, and that saved them.
No: night did not come on, so they were lost.
Not yet: they will be saved only if night comes on.
Yes, although night did not come on.
why: Right: εἰ μή + aorist indicative … ἄν + aorist indicative is a past contrary-to-fact condition, so both clauses are denied: night did come, and they were saved.
Contrary to fact: 'if night had not come on, they would not have been saved', so in fact it did.
Aorist indicatives with ἄν point to the past, not a future possibility.
The condition is εἰ μή: the night's coming is exactly what saved them.
r8.ablation: Only recognising the past contrary-to-fact pattern (εἰ μή + aorist indicative, ἄν + aorist indicative) reverses the surface negatives into 'night came; they were saved'.

c1.greek: μάχῃ δὲ νικήσας ὁ Κλέαρχος τὸ χωρίον ___.
accepted: εἷλε
εἷλεν

c2.greek: οἱ δὲ κωμῆται τοῖς Ἕλλησι σῖτον καὶ οἶνον ___.

c3.greek: ὁ δὲ κατάσκοπος ὑπὸ τῶν φυλάκων ___.

c5.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν λόφον ἀφίκετο, ὁ στρατηγὸς ___ καὶ ἐσκόπει τοὺς πολεμίους.

c6.greek: τῶν δὲ πολεμίων ___, οἱ Ἕλληνες εἰς τάξιν καθίσταντο.
c6.meaning_en: as the enemy were approaching / came up
accepted: προσιόντων
προσερχομένων
προσελθόντων

c8.notes: After a past main verb (κατέστησεν) Attic uses either the optative (φύγοι) or the 'vivid' subjunctive (φύγῃ); aorist and present aspect are both grammatical, and the compound ἀποφεύγω gives the same meaning. p3.label: Plato, Apology 21a–b
p3.source: Perseus tlg0059.tlg002.perseus-grc2 21a–b (canonical-greekLit; Burnet OCT text), from καὶ ἴστε δὴ to ἐτραπόμην
p3.context_en: Socrates is defending himself before an Athenian jury in 399 BC. He has just mentioned his old friend Chaerephon, now dead.

sentences.translation_en: And you know what sort of man Chaerephon was, how impetuous in whatever he set out to do.

clauses.label: indirect question: what sort of man Chaerephon was
relative: in whatever he set out to do

sentences.translation_en: And once he actually went to Delphi and dared to put this question to the oracle — and, as I say, don't make an uproar, gentlemen — he asked, you see, whether anyone was wiser than me.

clauses.label: parenthesis: and, as I say, don't make an uproar, gentlemen
indirect question: whether anyone was wiser than me

sentences.translation_en: Well, the Pythia answered that no one was wiser.

clauses.label: indirect statement: that no one was wiser

sentences.translation_en: And about these things his brother here will testify to you, since he himself has died.
Now consider why I am telling you this:

clauses.label: relative/indirect question: for what reasons I say this

sentences.translation_en: for I am going to show you where the prejudice against me has come from.

clauses.label: indirect question: where the prejudice against me has come from

sentences.translation_en: For when I heard this, I kept turning it over like this:
'What on earth does the god mean, and what is he hinting at?
For I am not conscious of being wise in anything, great or small.

clauses.label: participle (what I am conscious of): of being wise

sentences.translation_en: What on earth, then, does he mean by asserting that I am the wisest?

clauses.label: indirect statement: that I am the wisest

sentences.translation_en: For surely he is not lying, at any rate;
that is not permitted to him.'

clauses.label: impersonal construction; ἐστί and ψεύδεσθαι understood

sentences.translation_en: And for a long time I was at a loss as to what he meant;
then, very reluctantly, I turned to investigating it, in some such way as this.

p3-q1.prompt_en: What did Chaerephon ask at Delphi, and what was the answer?
options: Whether anyone was wiser than Socrates; the answer was that no one was.
Whether Socrates was wiser than anyone; the answer was that he was not.
Who was wiser than Socrates; the answer named Chaerephon himself.
Whether anyone was wiser than Socrates; the answer was 'no one but the god'.
why: Right: ἐμοῦ is a genitive of comparison after σοφώτερος, and μηδένα is the subject of εἶναι.
That reverses the comparison: the question is whether anyone (τις) was wiser than him (ἐμοῦ).
εἰ introduces a yes/no question ('whether'), and the reply names nobody.
The Pythia's reply is just μηδένα σοφώτερον εἶναι; the god is not mentioned in it.
p3-q1.ablation: Who is compared with whom depends on reading ἐμοῦ as a genitive of comparison and τις / μηδένα as subjects; ignore the cases and B is as good as A.

p3-q2.prompt_en: Why, according to Socrates, is he telling the jury this story?
options: To show them where the prejudice against him came from
To prove to them that he is the wisest of men
To show them what a reckless man Chaerephon was
To explain why the god is angry with Athens
why: Right: σκέψασθε δὴ ὧν ἕνεκα ταῦτα λέγω· μέλλω γὰρ … διδάξειν ὅθεν μοι ἡ διαβολὴ γέγονεν. The γάρ gives the reason.
He goes on to say he is not aware of being wise at all; the story explains the διαβολή.
Chaerephon's character is an aside (οἷος ἦν Χαιρεφῶν), not the point of the story.
Nothing is said about the god's anger.
p3-q2.ablation: The link between the oracle story and the διαβολή is made only by ὧν ἕνεκα and the explanatory γάρ; without them, B (a story about the oracle proving his wisdom) is the natural reading.

p3-q3.prompt_en: Why is Socrates puzzled by the oracle?
options: He is not conscious of being wise in anything, great or small, yet the god calls him the wisest.
He knows he is wise in small matters but not in great ones, yet the god calls him the wisest.
He is aware of being wise, but others say he knows nothing.
He knows that the god is wise in all things, great and small, yet speaks in riddles.
why: Right: οὔτε μέγα οὔτε σμικρὸν negates σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ σοφὸς ὤν: he is not conscious of being wise in anything, great or small.
οὔτε … οὔτε denies both: neither in great things nor in small.
The participle phrase is negated; and others' opinion does not come in until later.
The nominative σοφὸς ὤν goes with ἐγώ, the subject of σύνοιδα, not with the god.
p3-q3.ablation: The content of Socrates's self-knowledge is in the supplementary participle σοφὸς ὤν after σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ, under οὔτε … οὔτε; attach it to the god (D) or misread the double negative (B, C) and the puzzle changes.

p3-q4.prompt_en: Socrates says: οὐ γὰρ δήπου ψεύδεταί γε· οὐ γὰρ θέμις αὐτῷ. What do these words do in his reasoning?
options: They rule out the easy way out (that the god is simply lying), so the puzzle stands.
They suggest that the god may well be lying, which would solve the puzzle.
They state Socrates's conclusion that he really is the wisest of men.
They report what the Pythia said when Chaerephon pressed her further.
why: Right: οὐ … δήπου … γε is 'surely he is not lying, of course', and the second γάρ gives the ground (it is not permitted to him).
δήπου with οὐ marks the idea as obviously false, not as a live possibility.
The next sentence says he was at a loss for a long time: no conclusion has been reached.
These are Socrates's own thoughts (ἐνεθυμούμην οὑτωσί), not the Pythia's words.
p3-q4.ablation: The learner must recognise that ruling out divine falsehood leaves the oracle's meaning unresolved; this item does not independently diagnose understanding of δήπου or γε.

p4.source: Perseus tlg0085.tlg005.perseus-grc2 lines 1–6, 8–11 (canonical-greekLit; Smyth 1926 text). Line 7, bracketed as spurious in that edition and deleted by most editors, is left out; the printed τό in line 8 is corrected to τὸ. A full stop is supplied after line 6 following omission of line 7.

word_help.en: the sons of Atreus (Agamemnon and Menelaus)

p4.context_en: The opening of Aeschylus's Agamemnon (458 BC): a watchman speaks, alone, at night, in Argos. (Line 7, which most editors delete, is left out.)

sentences.translation_en: (1) I ask the gods for release from these toils,
(2) a year-long watch in length, during which, lying

clauses.label: apposition: (release from) a year-long watch's length
relative: during which (its verb is κάτοιδα, line 4)

tokens.gloss: on the roof (poetic dative of place; prose ἐπὶ τῆς στέγης)
on my elbows (poetic; some take it as 'up aloft')

sentences.translation_en: (3) on the roof of the Atreidae, on my elbows, like a dog,

clauses.label: participle phrase (cont.): on the roof… like a dog

sentences.translation_en: (4) I have come to know the assembly of the night's stars,

clauses.label: relative clause (cont.), its verb κάτοιδα: I know well the stars' assembly

sentences.translation_en: (5) and those that bring winter and summer to mortals,

clauses.label: second object of κάτοιδα: and those that bring winter and summer…

tokens.gloss: in the upper air, the sky

sentences.translation_en: (6) the bright lords, conspicuous in the sky. [Line 7 is omitted.]
(8) And now I am watching for the beacon's signal,
(9) the blaze of fire bringing word from Troy

clauses.label: apposition to σύμβολον: the blaze of fire

tokens.gloss: of capture (poetic: 'telling of the city's fall')

sentences.translation_en: (10) and tidings of its capture; for so commands

clauses.label: participle's second object: and tidings of capture

sentences.translation_en: (11) a woman's expectant heart, that plans like a man's.

clauses.label: subject of κρατεῖ (line 10): a woman's man-counselling, expectant heart

p4-q1.prompt_en: Where and how has the watchman spent his year of nights?
options: Lying on the roof of the Atreidae's palace, like a dog
Curled up inside the Atreidae's palace, beside the dogs
On the palace roof, keeping watch over the Atreidae's dogs
At the city gate, lying awake like the Atreidae's guard-dog
why: Right: στέγαις Ἀτρειδῶν is a dative of place ('on the roof of the Atreidae'), and κυνὸς δίκην is 'like a dog'.
στέγαις (στέγη 'roof') puts him on top of the building, and the dog is a comparison, not company.
κυνὸς δίκην (δίκην + genitive) means 'in the manner of a dog'; he is not guarding dogs.
στέγαις Ἀτρειδῶν is the palace roof, not a gate.
p4-q1.ablation: The place depends on the bare dative στέγαις (a poetic dative of place, no preposition) and the manner on the adverbial accusative δίκην + genitive; misread either case and B or C follow.

p4-q2.prompt_en: What exactly is he watching for now?
options: A beacon's signal: a blaze of fire bringing word from Troy, news of its capture
A torch to be carried from Troy by a messenger announcing its capture
The bright stars that bring news of winter and summer to mortals
A fire at Troy that would tell the Trojans the Greeks were captured
why: Right: αὐγὴν πυρός stands in apposition to λαμπάδος τὸ σύμβολον, and φέρουσαν (feminine) agrees with αὐγήν: the fire itself brings the news.
φέρουσαν agrees with αὐγήν (the blaze), so the fire is the bringer; no messenger is mentioned.
The stars belong to the previous sentence (what he has come to know); καὶ νῦν turns to what he waits for.
ἐκ Τροίας: the word comes from Troy to Argos, and ἁλώσιμον is about Troy's capture.
p4-q2.ablation: φέρουσαν must be attached to αὐγήν (feminine accusative) and φάτιν / βάξιν taken as its objects; detach the participle and the bringer could be a messenger (B) or the stars (C).

p4-q3.prompt_en: Why is he keeping this watch, according to the last two lines?
options: A woman with a man's will, full of expectation, commands it.
He hopes to win a woman's heart by bringing the news.
A man who plans like a woman rules the palace.
The men of the house hope that the woman will soon rule.
why: Right: κέαρ ('heart', neuter) is the subject of κρατεῖ; ἀνδρόβουλον and ἐλπίζον (neuter) agree with it; γυναικός says whose heart.
The heart is the subject that commands, not something to be won; ἐλπίζον belongs to the heart.
ἀνδρόβουλον agrees with κέαρ ('a heart of manly counsel'), and the heart is a woman's (γυναικός).
κρατεῖ is present: she already commands; ἐλπίζον describes her heart, not the men's hope.
p4-q3.ablation: Only the neuter agreement of ἀνδρόβουλον and ἐλπίζον with κέαρ, and γυναικός as its genitive, says whose heart commands and which is 'man-counselling'; without it, B–D are possible arrangements of the same words.

p2b.label: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.5.11–13
p2b.context_en: Cyrus's army is camped by a river in Mesopotamia; Clearchus and Menon each command a contingent of Greek mercenaries.

tokens.gloss: do wrong, be in the wrong

sentences.translation_en: When some of Menon's soldiers and some of Clearchus's had a dispute here about something, Clearchus, judging Menon's man to be in the wrong, gave him a beating;
and he went to his own contingent and told them;
and the soldiers, hearing it, were indignant and violently angry with Clearchus.
On the same day Clearchus, having gone to the river crossing and inspected the market there, rides off to his own tent through Menon's camp, with a few of his attendants;
Cyrus had not yet arrived, but was still riding up;
and one of Menon's soldiers who was splitting wood, when he saw Clearchus riding through, lets fly at him with his axe;
and this man missed him;
but another (threw) a stone, and another, then many, as a shout went up.
He takes refuge with his own troops, and at once passes the order 'to arms';

His hoplites he ordered to stay where they were, resting their shields against their knees, while he himself, taking the Thracians and the horsemen who were with him in the army, more than forty, most of them Thracians, charged at Menon's men, so that they were panic-struck, Menon himself too, and ran to their arms;
and some just stood there, at a loss what to make of it.

p2b-q1.prompt_en: What happens in this passage, in brief?
options: A quarrel among two generals' soldiers nearly turns into a fight between their whole contingents.

p2b-q5.ablation: The effect is in the ὥστε + infinitive clause; without recognising it as a result clause, the following sentence (οἱ δὲ … ἕστασαν) or the charge itself is an equally tempting span.

w1b.prompt_en: Tell this part of the story as Clearchus, in the first person: what happened to you as you rode through Menon's camp, and what did you do next? One or two Greek sentences.
model_answers: διελαύνοντί μοι διὰ τοῦ Μένωνος στρατεύματος στρατιώτης τις ἧκε τὴν ἀξίνην· ἐγὼ δὲ κατέφυγον εἰς τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ στράτευμα καὶ εὐθὺς παρήγγειλα εἰς τὰ ὅπλα.
ἐπεὶ διὰ τοῦ Μένωνος στρατεύματος ἤλαυνον, ἔβαλλόν με λίθοις· ἐγὼ δὲ κατέφυγον πρὸς τοὺς ἐμαυτοῦ στρατιώτας.
w1b.rubric: Communication: (1) Menon's men threw an axe / stones at Clearchus as he rode through; (2) he took refuge with his own troops and called them to arms. Forms looked at: first-person singular aorists (κατέφυγον 2nd aorist; παρήγγειλα liquid aorist), the first-person pronoun as object or dative (με, μοι), and the reflexive ἐμαυτοῦ for 'my own'.
